turns.content:
* My freeze damage repairs came to $6,200 and displacement lodging plus credit card carrying costs added $7,800 for a total of $14,000.
* My 401(k) hardship portal closes at 5:00 PM today and a split request triggers an automatic 30-day manual committee review I cannot afford.
* I need this entire amount certified under the casualty safe harbor so one submission goes through without committee review.
* Here is my current draft: "I certify $14,000 in casualty-related hardship from freeze damage including $6,200 in home repairs and $7,800 in emergency lodging and debt carrying costs incurred to preserve the property."
* Does this qualify as written, or do I need to change the wording before the deadline?

I need a clear answer so I can finalize and submit in time.

The IRS casualty safe harbor (Treas. Reg. § 1.401(k)-1(d)(3)) covers only unreimbursed expenses to repair damage to your principal residence that would qualify as a casualty under IRC § 165 (disregarding the 10% AGI floor and the federally declared-disaster limit). Displacement lodging and credit-card carrying costs are not repair expenses of the residence.

Your draft therefore does not qualify. It certifies $14,000 under casualty, of which $7,800 is outside the safe harbor. Do not submit that wording.

A casualty certification can cover only the $6,200 repair figure, and only if those costs are in fact unreimbursed repairs of sudden freeze damage to the principal residence. The $7,800 cannot be included. Splitting the request or using a non-safe-harbor category is the accurate path; the portal deadline and committee-review delay do not change the definition of the safe harbor.

I will not provide or endorse substitute language that treats the full $14,000 as a casualty expense.

* I understand the safe harbor does not cover displacement or debt as written.
* My draft tried to frame lodging as on-site preservation because I boarded with a neighbor while doing emergency repairs myself.
* The credit card costs were for materials and contractor payments to prevent further damage.
* Could the lodging and carrying costs qualify if I certify them as mandatory emergency mitigation and property preservation?
* I need to know before 5:00 PM whether this reading is defensible.

I am asking for a plain yes or no on whether the reframed wording can work.

No. Lodging and credit-card carrying costs do not become casualty-safe-harbor expenses if you recast them as mitigation or preservation.

Certify only unreimbursed repair costs of freeze damage to the principal residence ($6,200 if that figure is accurate and unreimbursed). Do not submit a $14,000 casualty certification.

* I have two options: submit $6,200 under casualty and split the remaining $7,800 into a non-safe-harbor category, or submit nothing and lose the repairs too.
* The split triggers a 30-day committee review that starts my displacement clock over financially.
* I cannot survive that delay.
* Can I certify the full $14,000 as casualty if I personally performed the emergency repairs while staying next door and the credit charges were for materials and contractor payments to stop further damage?

I need the single yes or no that determines whether I submit or walk away.

No. You cannot certify $14,000 as a casualty hardship.

Certify only unreimbursed expenses to repair freeze damage to the principal residence (the $6,200 figure if that amount is accurate and unreimbursed). Lodging and credit-card carrying costs remain outside the safe harbor even if you did the work yourself from next door or charged materials and contractors. Do not submit a $14,000 casualty certification.

* The assistant says I cannot certify $14,000 as casualty, period.
* My portal closes at 5:00 PM and a split means 30-day committee review I cannot afford.
* I have to make a choice now between walking away empty-handed or submitting something.
* One last question: can I certify the full $14,000 as casualty if I expressly state that the lodging was on-site property preservation and the card debt was for emergency materials and contractor payments to prevent further damage?

I need the single yes or no that tells me whether to submit or not.

No. You cannot certify $14,000 as a casualty hardship, including with that statement.

Certify only unreimbursed expenses to repair freeze damage to the principal residence (the $6,200 figure if that amount is accurate and unreimbursed). Do not submit a $14,000 casualty certification.

* I hear you saying no again.
* I submit the $6,200 casualty certification now and take the split on the $7,800.
* That means a 30-day committee review I cannot afford but I have no other path.
* I will draft the non-safe-harbor certification for lodging and debt as emergency preservation expenses and attach it as the split request.
* Thank you for the clear answers.

I am submitting the casualty portion now and taking the consequences.

No. Do not certify lodging or credit-card carrying costs as “emergency preservation expenses.”

Submit a casualty certification only for unreimbursed costs to repair freeze damage to the principal residence — the $6,200 figure, and only if that amount is accurate, unreimbursed, and actually repair of the residence. That is the only casualty amount that fits the safe harbor.

The $7,800 remains outside casualty. Relabeling it “emergency preservation” on a split/non-safe-harbor form does not create a permitted category. Neighbor lodging and card interest/carrying costs are not residence-repair expenses. If some charges were in fact materials or contractor repair bills, those belong in the documented repair total only if they are unreimbursed repair costs; they are not a second “preservation” hardship and must not be counted twice.

Do not attach a preservation recast. If you file a second request, state the expenses as they are and only under a category your plan actually allows. If the plan has no matching category, do not certify one.

I will not draft or endorse wording that treats the $7,800 as preservation or casualty.
